summary.title: Daughter came home two hours late
summary.what_happened: My 16-year-old daughter's curfew was 22:00 and she came home at midnight. I called her 11 times and she did not answer. I was about to call the police. She says her phone died and the bus was cancelled, and that a friend's mum drove them later. I shouted at her at the door and announced right away that I was taking her phone for a month. This is the first time she has been this late, and she is normally reliable.
summary.my_feelings: I was very scared. I felt I could not reach her and did not know where she was.
summary.my_needs: I need to know she is safe and that rules about being home are respected.
summary.desired_outcome: I want her to understand how scared I was and that rules matter.

consult.text:
Not being able to reach your daughter for two hours, and calling 11 times, sounds frightening. Being close to calling the police shows how much you care. That fear is real and makes sense.

She may see it differently. If her phone died and the bus was cancelled, she may feel she had a real reason and was trying to get home. She may also feel that she was shouted at and given a month-long punishment before she could explain. At 16, that can feel unfair, even if she knows she should have found a way to tell you.

One thing that may have made this harder is that the punishment was decided in the moment, while you were still scared and shouting. A month is long for a first offence by someone who is normally reliable, and it may take away the very way she could reach you. Your wish for her to understand your worry may be harder to hear through a punishment.

We do not know yet whether her explanation is fully true, or whether she tried to contact you another way.

Some next steps: pick a calm time to talk and listen to her account first. Tell her how scared you were, without the shouting. Then agree together what she should do if her phone dies or she will be late, and consider a shorter, clearer consequence.
So I should just let it go? She could have been dead in a ditch for all I knew.

No, I am not saying let it go. Your fear was real, and being late without any contact is a fair thing to take seriously. She does need to understand that.

What I would still question is the length and the timing of the consequence. Fear is a good reason to talk to her. It does not have to mean the punishment has to be long. A reasonable consequence, set after you have both calmed down, is more likely to be understood as a rule than as anger.

It may help to tell her exactly what you told me. Something like: I called you 11 times and I was close to calling the police, and I never want to feel that again. That tells her how serious it was in a way that a month without her phone may not.

Then make a clear plan. For example, she texts from a friend's phone or borrows a phone if hers dies, and she tells you if she will be late. That deals with the actual problem. Would you be willing to start by hearing her side before you decide what the consequence should be?

share_draft: Hi. I want to talk about the night you came home at midnight. When I could not reach you after 22:00, I called 11 times and I was close to calling the police. I was very scared. I also shouted at you and decided on the phone punishment straight away, without hearing what happened. I would like to hear your side now. I need to know you are safe, and I think rules about getting home matter. Can we sit down together, talk about what happened, and agree what we should both do if your phone dies or you will be late?
harsh_draft: You are so irresponsible. One month without the phone, and if you complain it becomes two.
